report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions.
At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale.
In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions.

Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner's behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors).

We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework's flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.
Adequately describing, understanding, and predicting an individual's behavior during social interactions are fundamental tasks for the behavioral sciences [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] .
text.formatted: Adequately describing, understanding, and predicting an individual's behavior during social interactions are fundamental tasks for the behavioral sciences <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> .

text.text: How people perceive, respond to, and act toward others in social interactions largely defines their personality, drives individual development, and has short-, medium-, and long-term consequences for well-being, relationship qualities, and a variety of life outcomes 1, 4, [6] [7] [8] [9] .
text.formatted: How people perceive, respond to, and act toward others in social interactions largely defines their personality, drives individual development, and has short-, medium-, and long-term consequences for well-being, relationship qualities, and a variety of life outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> .

text.text: While individual differences in social interactions are a focal topic of the behavioral sciences with a range of theoretical frameworks and empirical findings [1] [2] [3] [4] 7, 8, 10, 11 , there is a lack of computational models that formalize how these differences dynamically emerge and manifest during interactions.
text.formatted: While individual differences in social interactions are a focal topic of the behavioral sciences with a range of theoretical frameworks and empirical findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , there is a lack of computational models that formalize how these differences dynamically emerge and manifest during interactions.

text.text: Among the most comprehensive and established frameworks in social interaction research is contemporary integrative interpersonal theory (CIIT) 3, 11, 12 , which conceptualizes personality expression as unfolding dynamically within social interactions.
text.formatted: Among the most comprehensive and established frameworks in social interaction research is contemporary integrative interpersonal theory (CIIT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , which conceptualizes personality expression as unfolding dynamically within social interactions.

text.text: CIIT provides a coherent framework not only for general patterns of interaction dynamics such as the degree to which the behavior of interacting individuals is (dis)similar (complementarity) but also for describing, understanding, and predicting individual differences in social interaction.
This includes both differences in people's baseline levels of interpersonal behavior (behavioral defaults) and differences in how they respond to others' behavior (interpersonal reactivities).
Individuals vary substantially in both their behavioral defaults and their interpersonal reactivities 1, [13] [14] [15] [16] , and these differences critically shape how social interactions unfold.
text.formatted: Individuals vary substantially in both their behavioral defaults and their interpersonal reactivities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> , and these differences critically shape how social interactions unfold.

text.text: Despite its extensive empirical foundation, CIIT lacks integrative formal models that unify these phenomena within a single framework and capture how they unfold dynamically between interacting individuals 1, 12, 17, 18 .
text.formatted: Despite its extensive empirical foundation, CIIT lacks integrative formal models that unify these phenomena within a single framework and capture how they unfold dynamically between interacting individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Although there are conceptually rich descriptions regarding the mechanisms through which behavioral defaults and interpersonal reactivities contribute to differences in interpersonal behavior, these mechanisms remain mathematically underspecified.
Agent-based modeling (ABM) is one important method for formalizing such mechanisms and simulating their dynamics [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: Agent-based modeling (ABM) is one important method for formalizing such mechanisms and simulating their dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> .

text.text: However, the resulting interpersonal behavior in ABMs is abstract (i.e., only numbers) and lacks usability and ecological validity.
Recent advances in artificial intelligence offer novel opportunities to bridge this gap 20, 24, 25.
text.formatted: Recent advances in artificial intelligence offer novel opportunities to bridge this gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref>.

text.text: Embedding the principles of CIIT into an ABM framework powered by large language models (LLMs) makes it possible to simulate, assess, and manipulate social interactions with linguistic realism, systematic parameter variation, and scalability [24] [25] [26] .
text.formatted: Embedding the principles of CIIT into an ABM framework powered by large language models (LLMs) makes it possible to simulate, assess, and manipulate social interactions with linguistic realism, systematic parameter variation, and scalability <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> .

text.text: It enables formalizing how individual differences shape interpersonal dynamics while expressing those dynamics in natural-language interactions.

CIIT conceptualizes personality as inherently relational: emerging, expressed, and understood within social interactions 2, 3, 11, 12, 27 and organizes personality expression along two orthogonal dimensions: agency and communion 11, 28 .
text.formatted: CIIT conceptualizes personality as inherently relational: emerging, expressed, and understood within social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> and organizes personality expression along two orthogonal dimensions: agency and communion <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Agency characterizes individuals in terms of influence, control, and mastery, ranging from dominant to submissive.
Communion characterizes how individuals relate to others in terms of closeness, intimacy, and affiliation, ranging from friendly to hostile.

These dimensions define the interpersonal circumplex (IPC), a circular structural model originating from Leary's 29 interpersonal circle and further developed to locate interpersonal traits, motives, and behaviors within a two-dimensional space 28, 30 .
text.formatted: These dimensions define the interpersonal circumplex (IPC), a circular structural model originating from Leary's <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> interpersonal circle and further developed to locate interpersonal traits, motives, and behaviors within a two-dimensional space <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: CIIT situates the components through which personality unfolds in real time (i.e., dispositions, situational perceptions, momentary goals, and self-related or affective processes) within this agency-communion space 3, 11, 12, 27 .
text.formatted: CIIT situates the components through which personality unfolds in real time (i.e., dispositions, situational perceptions, momentary goals, and self-related or affective processes) within this agency-communion space <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: In this study, we focus on behavior, through which these processes become observable in interactions.

To describe how interpersonal behavior unfolds in "interpersonal situations" 2, 3, 27 , CIIT draws on the transaction cycle 31, 32 , a causal loop in which each individual's behavior, and their perception of the partner's behavior, reciprocally influence one another over the course of an interaction (Fig. 1).

text.text: The transaction cycle provides both a conceptual foundation for modeling social interactions as a cyclical process and a mechanism for explaining moment-to-moment changes in interpersonal behavior.
Despite its conceptual clarity, there are remarkably few formal models that build directly on CIIT, instantiate its transactional logic, and account for the unfolding of interpersonal dynamics.
Westermann and Banisch 18 proposed a "relational state space" model that to our knowledge constitutes the first CIIT-consistent account to formalize interpersonal dynamics.

text.text: They defined a tetrahedral (four-sided) space of dyadic relations and demonstrated how different configurations of affiliative approach and avoidance motives yield interpersonal patterns.
Yet, their relational state space is a dyad-level construct which offers only limited possibilities for incorporating person-specific parameters at scale.
To move toward models that integrate individual differences, it is essential to identify and formalize the phenomena that shape how interpersonal behavior evolves over the course of an interaction.

Drawing on CIIT and empirical findings from social interaction research 6, 9, 15, [33] [34] [35] [36] , we focus on two key individual difference variables: behavioral defaults and interpersonal reactivities.

text.text: Behavioral defaults capture differences in the baseline behavioral level with which individuals enter social interactions and toward which their behavior tends to return over time.

Within the IPC, behavioral defaults correspond to a person's typical location on the agentic and communal axes in the absence of strong situational influences, especially the interaction partner's behavior.

Empirically, such defaults are typically approximated by individuals' characteristic distributions of behavioral states across situations (e.g., their average level of agency or communion across repeated observations), although observed behavior also reflects influences from the interaction partner.
Previous studies have shown substantial individual differences in behavioral defaults across different kinds of behaviors in general 37, 38 and for agency and communion in particular 13, 33 .

text.text: These differences are reliably measurable and highly stable over time 13, 37, 38 , whereas deviations from these defaults (i.e., "acting out of character") have been associated with negative outcomes such as reduced positive affect and increased psychological depletion 39 .

text.text: Integrating both behavioral defaults and interpersonal reactivities is therefore an important step to describe, understand, and predict social interactions.
Doing so requires specifying the processes through which differences in interpersonal behavior unfold over time.
In recent years, psychological science has increasingly emphasized formal models as a tool to make theoretical assumptions precise and to derive testable predictions 23, 47 .

text.text: This approach is particularly promising for social interaction research 1, 18, 21, 41, 48 , where many theoretical frameworks provide detailed descriptions of key concepts and relationships in natural language but are not typically specified in mathematical terms 1, 2, 12, 17, 18, 23 .

text.text: Existing efforts to model social interactions based on CIIT have primarily focused on specific phenomena, most notably complementarity 35, 44, 45, 49, 50 , and have not yet yielded fully formalized, generative, and predictive models of interpersonal dynamics, with Westermann and Banisch 18 providing a notable exception.

text.text: Thus, despite the availability of theoretical blueprints and methodological tools for formal models of social interactions 10, 21, 22, 47 , the systematic implementation and evaluation of formal models of interpersonal behavior remains limited.

text.text: A limitation of classical ABM, however, is that agents exchange only numbers or heavily simplified patterns of interpersonal behavior.

This keeps formal-model evaluation tractable but cannot capture the richness of interpersonal behavior, in particular the dynamics central to CIIT and the interpretation of language that underpins social interaction 20, 24, 25 , and it constrains both realistic simulations and human-model interaction.

text.text: Existing approaches to simulating differences in interpersonal behavior with LLMs are limited in two ways.
First, most work implements personality expression as a fixed trait level 56, 57 and assesses it from one-time textual input 58, 59 or explicit self-descriptions 59.

Adequately simulating ecologically valid interactions and deriving insights for formal-model and theory development therefore require LLM-based simulations that capture and adapt to the partner's momentary interpersonal behavior and that connect an explicit formal model steering behavior across the interaction with the language capabilities of LLMs.

text.text: In this study, we aim to make three core contributions: (1) Introducing an overarching framework for LLM-based Agent Simulations of individual differences in Social Interactions (LASSI), in which each agent's interpersonal behavior is continually adjusted in response to the perceived behavior of the interaction partner.

(2) Developing and implementing a mathematical model that formalizes how two key individual difference variables (i.e., behavioral defaults, interpersonal reactivities) jointly shape an agent's interpersonal behavior and verifying its behavior in numerical simulations.
(3) Demonstrating how LASSI translates interpersonal dynamics into natural language and outlining applications across the behavioral sciences.

text.text: Each LLM-based agent consists of two distinct components: a generator, responsible for simulating interpersonal behavior, and an assessor, responsible for assessing the interpersonal behavior expressed by the interaction partner.
This division maps onto the two separate but interrelated components of expressing and perceiving behavior that are central to humans in social interactions 10.

text.text: A central design principle of LASSI is to keep the formal modeling of interpersonal dynamics separate from the realistic language generation via the LLMs.
The formal model defines how an agent's interpersonal state (i.e., agency and communion) evolves independently of any linguistic realization.
An LLM-based generator renders a sampled interpersonal state as a concrete natural-language utterance, whereas an LLM-based assessor maps an observed utterance back onto agency and communion.
Thus, the language model provides linguistic and contextual realism, usability through human users, and scalability, not the interpersonal dynamics themselves.
LASSI's components can be evaluated separately: the formal model on its numerical output alone, the generator and assessor independently of the formal model, and the full pipeline end to end.

The figure depicts one iteration of this cycle, an interaction exchange.
Each exchange comprises two interaction turns, in which each agent assesses the partner's behavior, updates its internal state according to a formal model, and generates behavior.
Prior to the interaction, each agent's behavioral repertoire is initialized for both IPC dimensions, agency and communion.
Without prior interaction history or context, the repertoire's mean is set to the agent's behavioral default.
A discrete state is then sampled from it to start the interaction.
Based on this state, Agent-A's generator is prompted to express behavior aligned with the sampled state's position in the interpersonal space.

The generator's system prompt combines a static part (the interaction context, background information, and instructions to remain in character) with a dynamic part that describes the agent's current states on both dimensions (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2).

Agent-A's assessor then rates this message, and Agent-A's repertoire is updated accordingly.

text.text: Overview of the dyadic interaction cycle for simulating social interactions.
The figure shows one iteration of the cycle, an interaction exchange, in an agent-agent interaction; the dynamic prompts are paraphrased and abbreviated for display.
A formal model governs the dynamics in LASSI (see Methods for details).
It updates each agent's interpersonal behavior from turn to turn, each interpersonal dimension independently.
An agent's behavior is modeled as draws from a behavioral repertoire, a probability distribution of width τ over a symmetric scale centered at zero.
The mean of this repertoire is anchored at the behavioral default (BD) and shifted by the partner as the interaction unfolds.

Interpersonal reactivity (IR) is a single parameter between -1 and +1 whose magnitude sets how much influence the partner's behavior has and whose sign sets whether the agent responds complementarily or against complementarity.
At each turn the agent forms a partner-implied target.
If IR is positive, that means mirroring (i.e., opposing) the partner on agency and matching the partner on communion.
The agent blends this target with its default in proportion to |IR|, and then moves part of the way toward that blend at a relaxation rate λ.
Behavior therefore shows turn-to-turn inertia, while relaxing back toward the default when the partner exerts little influence (|IR| near 0).
Each agent is thus described on each interpersonal dimension by four parameters: BD, IR, τ, and λ.
We ran numerical simulations to verify that the model produces two interpersonal dynamics: complementarity at the dyad level and flux at the individual level.
We also tested whether an agent's four person parameters (BD, IR, τ, and λ) could be recovered from simulated data.
For the interpersonal-dynamics simulations, λ was fixed at 0.5 (see Methods for the setup).

In this study, we introduced LASSI, a framework for simulating social interactions and individual differences therein using LLM-based agents grounded in CIIT.

By integrating behavioral defaults (BDs) and interpersonal reactivities (IRs) into a unified computational architecture, LASSI specifies how individual differences shape and are expressed in social interactions.
Numerical simulations showed that cross-lagged complementarity and flux emerged as expected from the model, with complementarity tracking each agent's IR and flux increasing with |IR|.
Parameter recovery was best for repertoire width (τ) and the direction of reactivity, moderate for the behavioral default (BD) and reactivity (IR), and weakest for the relaxation rate (λ).

Integrating the formal model into the full LASSI pipeline illustrated how its states are expressed in individual messages and how the resulting interpersonal dynamics appear in natural-language interactions.
In the following, we outline three major advantages of the LASSI framework.

First, its architecture is model-agnostic: it is not bound to any specific LLM, so current and future systems can be integrated, and it can be extended beyond text to voice, video, or virtual reality 66, 67 .

text.text: The present study establishes that the formal model behaves as specified and that its states can be rendered in natural language, but it does not yet establish that these dynamics or linguistic realizations accurately reproduce human interactions.
Validation against large-scale human interaction data is therefore a key next step.
The model's current assumptions also motivate several promising refinements and extensions.
The first concerns the temporal granularity of the dyadic cycle.
Each iteration currently consists of one message exchange, with the behavioral repertoire updated only after the partner's message is processed.
This is straightforward but may oversimplify real interaction 35, 45 .

text.text: CIIT suggests that people adjust their behavior in response to both their own and their partner's actions 3, 11, 31 , so it may help to update after both messages, potentially with different parameters.

text.text: In the numerical simulations, both agents responded to the partner's state from the previous exchange, producing complementarity across exchanges but not within them.
In human interactions, however, complementarity has also been observed in behavior coded at short intervals.

Rich or ambiguous behavior can also produce shifts on much shorter timescales, within a single message 35, 45 , which motivates event-based updates, such as detecting highly agentic or communal behavior, or time-based updates at fixed intervals.

text.text: Evaluating behavior message by message can further mislead, since a neutral follow-up may be read as a change when it merely reflects prior behavior.
More nuanced schemes could weight each message by its information content or prompt the models to infer the current state from the full interaction history.
A second extension concerns the assumption that behavioral defaults and interpersonal reactivities remain constant across interaction contexts.
Reactivity can vary with the interaction partner, and complementarity can depend on the setting and on role status 4, 42, 49 .

text.text: Context-specific parameters could capture this, though they complicate fitting and evaluation and should be introduced only where they yield meaningful gains in explanatory power.
A final extension concerns the IPC itself, which we model with only the two orthogonal dimensions of agency and communion on a fixed set of scale values.

Incorporating additional rotations of the circumplex axes, such as the blends at 45-degree angles, and their interpersonal adjectives in the prompts for the generator and the assessor could capture finer nuances 28, 30 .

text.text: Representing a circular space on a square grid is also an approximation: distance from the neutral midpoint depends on direction, so a blend of high agency and high communion counts as more extreme than either alone.
Polar or wrapped geometries, and finer or dynamically scaled values, are natural alternatives.
Beyond these refinements and extensions, LASSI offers practical applications across the behavioral sciences.
Other personality variables, such as the Big Five or HEXACO, can be incorporated where relevant to a particular application.

The models it hosts could transfer to work and organizational settings, such as negotiation, conflict resolution, and leadership training; healthcare, such as therapeutic conversations, diagnostic interviews, and clinician training; education, such as teacher training and classroom simulation; and broader sociotechnical applications, such as game design, virtual environments, and human-computer interaction.
A particularly direct use is personalization training, in which trainees interact with agents that differ in interpersonal behavior and learn to recognize and adapt to those differences.

Such training is already being applied in medical education 73 , where simulations train adaptive communication with patients of different interpersonal profiles, and similar uses look promising in psychotherapy training and other helping professions 74.

text.text: In sum, LASSI is a framework for simulating social interactions with LLM-based agents grounded in CIIT, in which each agent updates its interpersonal behavior in response to the perceived behavior of its partner.
Its formal model specifies how complementarity, behavioral defaults, and interpersonal reactivities jointly shape behavior over time.
Together this offers a bounded, transparent, and extensible foundation for formalizing interpersonal dynamics, and a basis for practical tools that simulate interpersonal behavior at scale.

We propose a formal model of social interactions that steers how the interaction unfolds in the LLM-based interpersonal simulations.

Specifically, the model formalizes how the agent's interpersonal behavior is updated from turn to turn on the basis of its prior behavior, the partner's behavior, and the influence of behavioral defaults and interpersonal reactivities.

We use numerical simulations to examine how well the model's parameters can be recovered from model-generated interaction data and how recovery depends on the amount of data, and whether the model produces expected interpersonal dynamics (i.e., flux, complementarity).
All assumptions the model makes are listed in the section "Formal model of interpersonal behavior" in the Supplementary Methods.
However, three deliberate modeling choices are worth stating upfront.
First, the updating depends only on the prior state and the partner's most recent behavior rather than the full interaction history.
This keeps the model tractable, but limits it to short-term interactions and neglects longer-term history and relationship formation.
Second, behavior lives on a finite grid.
This makes the dynamics explicit, easy to inspect, and implementable in the LLM-based simulations with our dynamic prompting approach, at the cost of limiting granularity.
Third, as implied by CIIT, agency and communion are modeled separately, but empirical work suggests that they can covary within individuals during social interactions 16, 72.

This section presents the mathematical detail of the formal model that steers the agents in LASSI.

Here, we particularly focus on why the baseline repertoire is positioned by exponential tilting, why the spread of expressed behavior narrows near the ends of the scale, the mathematics of the update in full, and the assumptions the model makes.
We then describe how the model parameters were recovered from simulated data and how the model relates to published complementarity coefficients, including the sweep across relaxation rates.
For simplicity, we state the model for one agent on one interpersonal dimension.
Agency and communion are updated separately and never enter each other's equations.
The only dimension-specific element is the sign that defines complementarity, otherwise, the updating is identical across dimensions.

text.text: Interpersonal behavior on one dimension takes one of a finite number of values.
Specifically, the state grid is symmetric and centered on zero: 𝑆 = $-(𝑁 -1) 2 , … , + (𝑁 -1) 2.
with 𝑁 odd, so that the grid has an exact midpoint 𝑠̄ = 0.
All work reported here uses 𝑁 = 7, so the states run from -3 to +3.
Thus, we explicitly constrain the range of interpersonal behavior an agent can express.
An agent's behavior at turn t is a probability distribution over the grid (the behavioral repertoire), and the behavior the agent expresses is one draw from this repertoire.
This is the model's central representational choice because it separates two aspects that a single value cannot capture: the level of a person's behavior, and how widely it varies around that level.
Accordingly, two agents with the same expected state can differ in how consistently their behavior stays near it, as determined by the width of the distribution.
The baseline repertoire is the distribution an agent falls back on when the partner exerts no influence.

It is characterized by two of the four person parameters: the behavioral default BD, which is the baseline the person returns to without partner influence, and the repertoire width τ, which is how widely the person varies around it.
The main text gives the shape of the baseline repertoire as a Gaussian kernel of width τ.
On an unbounded scale, placing the peak of that kernel at BD also places its mean at BD.
On a finite grid, however, the tail is truncated near the scale boundary, pulling the mean inward.
This discrepancy increases as the behavioral default approaches the end of the scale (Supplementary Table S8).

The response direction 𝑑 = sign(IR), with 𝑑 = +1 at IR = 0, where it has no effect, is a property of the person and determines whether the agent responds in the complementary or the opposite direction.

text.text: John Doe has a behavioral default of +2 on communion, a repertoire width of 1.5, a strong reactivity of +0.9 and a relaxation rate of 0.5.
His expected communion entering the turn is +1.55.

In plain terms: A highly reactive warm agent, met with cold behavior, ends the turn just below the midpoint of the scale after starting well above it.
The agent does not go all the way to the blended location of -1.60.
The relaxation rate keeps half of where he already was.
His own warm default keeps a tenth of the blend, because |IR| = 0.9 leaves a share of 0.1 for BD.
The baseline repertoire is then re-tilted to have this new mean, and the behavior he expresses is a draw from the updated behavioral repertoire.
The update determines where the mean of the repertoire should be, but it does not determine how the remaining probability mass should be distributed.

To define the full repertoire, the model therefore selects, among all distributions with the required mean, the one that is closest to the agent's baseline repertoire in terms of Kullback-Leibler divergence:
This is the information projection of the baseline repertoire onto the mean constraint (Csiszár, 1975).
The baseline repertoire is altered only as much as necessary to achieve the required mean.
Specifically, the projection is given by an exponential tilt of the baseline repertoire: with the normalizer and the tilt fixed by the mean constraint.
Because this is a one-parameter exponential family, the derivative of the tilted mean is the tilted variance:
The tilted mean is therefore strictly increasing in the tilt, and it runs from the lower end of the grid to the upper end as the tilt runs over the real line.
Thus, it is a bijection onto the open interval between the two ends, every strictly interior target mean is attained exactly at one finite tilt, and no approximation enters.
At either end the only distribution with that mean is the point mass there, and that point mass is the projection.
In simple terms, the model can therefore move the repertoire exactly to any mean within the scale with a unique amount of tilting.

We checked this guarantee; over the full set of simulations, across 1,272 scored cells, the largest difference between the realized mean and the intended mean was 1.0 × 10⁻¹², the tolerance within which a target counts as lying on a scale end; all other cells stayed below 1 × 10⁻¹³.

text.text: This is a consequence of bounded behavior: as a person approaches the extreme of the scale, there is less room for variation, and the model captures this.

For interior repertoires, projecting onto the baseline repertoire or onto the previous turn's behavioral repertoire gives the same answer, which we verified to within 1 × 10⁻¹³ over 200 random five-step chains.
The tilted family is closed under tilting and the mean fixes the tilt uniquely, so the two routes coincide.
However, they differ in exactly one place.

After an agent has reached a scale end its distribution is a point mass, and the divergence from a point mass is infinite for every other distribution, so the second version would be trapped there for good.
We therefore project onto the baseline repertoire.

The tilt is found by safeguarded Newton iteration on the mean constraint, using the derivative identity above, with the bracket found by doubling outward from zero and a tolerance of 1 × 10⁻¹³ in grid units.
No fixed bracket is used.

The tilt required to move a baseline repertoire from its default to a given mean grows with 1/τ², without bound as τ shrinks, so any constant bracket silently rejects legitimate interior targets at some τ.
Below τ ≈ 0.11 on a unit-step grid the bracket search can reject an interior target, and below τ ≈ 0.08 a large share of targets is rejected; all reported work uses τ ≥ 0.25.
A BD exactly at a scale endpoint is excluded because it would make the baseline repertoire a point mass.
As the baseline repertoire serves as the reference distribution for all subsequent projections, this would prevent the agent from moving away from that endpoint.

text.text: These simulations also illustrate how study design affects separability of the parameters.
Conditions that keep agents close to their behavioral defaults contain little information for separating reactivity from the relaxation rate.
Conditions that move agents away from their defaults are more informative: on agency, this occurred for partners with similar defaults, and on communion for partners with opposite defaults.

-Please avoid vivid scene descriptions, stage directions, or explanatory third-person text.

-Even with more extreme personality levels, you behave largely normatively and respond appropriately to the situation.

-Later in the conversation, the topics can become more personal and deeper depending on how the interaction develops.
-Be creative and avoid repeating utterances as much as possible.

-Your personality should show through in an otherwise largely normative zero-acquaintance situation and should not be explained bluntly.

text.text: Interpersonal reactivity determines response direction and strength. a, Expected state after one exchange for an agent with a behavioral default of -2 interacting with a partner fixed at +1.

Agency and communion show opposite patterns because complementarity implies opposite target directions on the two dimensions. b, Resulting agency behavioral repertoires for IR = -1, -0.5, 0, +0.5, and +1. c, Agency trajectories across repeated exchanges with the same fixed partner.

Each trajectory approaches a stable point determined by the agent's behavioral default and the partner-implied target; the relaxation rate affects how quickly this point is reached, but not its location.
Seven-point grid, repertoire width = 1, relaxation rate = 0.5.
BD, behavioral default; IR, interpersonal reactivity; m, complementarity direction; T, partnerimplied target.
The agent first determines the state it would move to if it adjusted fully, weighting T against BD according to the magnitude |IR| of its reactivity:

With |IR| bounded between 0 and 1, this is a weighted average that always falls between BD and T. Interpersonal behavior is also autocorrelated from one moment to the next, so the expected state moves only part of the way toward that location, at the relaxation rate λ: 𝜇 -= (1 -𝜆)𝜇 -#4 + 𝜆 𝑞 - A small λ means strong inertia and slow adjustment.
A rate of 1 would move the expected state fully to 𝑞 - each turn, so that it would no longer depend on the previous expected state.
Combining these two steps gives the full update:
The three weights are (1 -𝜆), 𝜆(1 -|IR|), and 𝜆|IR|.
They are nonnegative and they sum to one, so the updated expected state is a convex combination of the previous state, the default, and the target.
In plain terms, a convex combination is a weighted average whose weights are shares of one whole.
At each turn the agent's expected state is therefore divided between three pulls, and the three shares always add up to one.
The first share is inertia, that is, where the agent already was.
The second is the pull back toward the agent's own behavioral default.
The third is the pull toward the partner-implied target.
This has two consequences: First, the expected state can never leave the range spanned by those three locations, so no rule is needed to keep behavior on the scale.

Second, the parameters read directly as competing influences on one turn: a highly reactive person gives most of its adjustable share to the partner, a barely reactive person keeps that share for its own default, and a person with a low relaxation rate gives most of the turn to where it already was.
The updated expected state is a convex combination of three locations that all lie within the range of the grid, so it cannot leave that range.
The simulations would have stopped on any excursion of more than 1 × 10⁻¹² outside the grid, and none did.
The guarantee rests on two conditions that hold throughout this study and are worth stating, because they are properties of the scale.
The complementarity direction m must be -1 or +1, and the scale midpoint s̄ must be the midpoint of the symmetric grid.
Move the midpoint off center and the target can leave the grid: at a midpoint of +1 on the -3 to +3 grid, a partner at -3 implies a target of +5 for a complementary responder on agency.
At zero reactivity the update becomes 𝜇 -= (1 -𝜆)𝜇 -#4 + 𝜆BD.
The behavioral default is the unique fixed point and the expected state returns to it geometrically at rate 1 -λ.
For any λ, an agent that starts from its own baseline repertoire therefore never moves at all.
At a fixed interior expected state, the width sets the spread and nothing else does: τ of 0.6, 1.0 and 1.5 gives realized standard deviations of 0.59, 1.00 and 1.41 at the midpoint of the scale.
The narrowing described in Supplementary Table S9 is a separate effect and applies to position, not to the width parameter.

text.text: At each turn the model forms the partner-implied target from the partner's last behavior, blends it with the agent's own behavioral default (BD) in proportion to the magnitude of the interpersonal reactivity (IR), and moves the expected state part of the way toward that blend at the relaxation rate λ.
It then tilts the agent's baseline repertoire to the new mean, retaining as much of its characteristic shape as possible.
By construction, the realized mean equals the intended mean and behavior remains within the scale.
The simultaneous coefficient is essentially zero at every relaxation rate.
In the simulations, both agents express a state and then update simultaneously.
Each agent therefore responds only to the partner's previous expressed state.
Conditional on the interaction history, the two same-turn draws are independent, and the mean dimension-aligned simultaneous coefficient across 1,210 scored cells was +0.0013.
Under this update schedule, the model therefore produces essentially no simultaneous complementarity.

This is an important limitation, because real interaction data can show simultaneous complementarity within short coding intervals; Kurzius et al. (2022) found it strongest within the same 10-s interval.
The model represents such mutual adjustment across separate turns.
In the population regression on the latent expected states, the stability coefficient equals one minus the relaxation rate.
For expressed states, it is strongly attenuated because the previous expressed state is only a noisy proxy for the previous latent mean (Supplementary Figs. S21-S24).

The latter falls below 0.5 because the estimated coefficient on a lagged outcome is biased downward in short series (Marriott & Pope,  1954).

The sweep shows that the model behaves consistently across relaxation rates, with lower rates predictably reducing the observed complementarity coefficient while preserving the same underlying dynamics.
What the sweep does not settle is which relaxation rate is most appropriate.
No value is better by an internal criterion.
The choice of 0.5 is motivated externally: at a rate of 1, an agent retains none of its prior state from one turn to the next, which is unlikely to reflect interpersonal behavior.

text.text: The first is the one-dimensional version of the distance score proposed by Woods and Wright (2024), defined as the negative distance from the complementary target and therefore bounded above by zero.
The second is the correlation between an agent's state and the same target.
It is signed, with +1 indicating perfect complementarity, 0 no association, and -1 perfect anti-complementarity.
We report the correlation alongside the distance score because the distance score alone cannot separate an anti-complementary dyad from a weakly complementary one.
Both scores compare an agent's expressed states with the complementary target, m times the partner's state, which is the same for every agent.
An anti-complementary agent therefore receives a low score.
Comparing each agent with its own partner-implied target T, which carries the agent's own sign d, would give every agent a high score, whatever its response direction.

At λ = 1, the model's update implies the Level-1 equation of Kurzius et al. (2022) exactly in the population regression, with 𝑏4 = 𝑏 ' = 0 and a dimension-aligned cross-lagged coefficient equal to IR.
Below 1, the coefficient in the update is λ × IR.
In the simulations, the fitted coefficients closely matched the expected value, with slopes ranging from 0.489 to 0.503 at λ = 0.5.
The small deviations reflect sampling variability and the use of the previous expressed state instead of the latent state.

This section documents the configuration of the two LLM-based agents used in the manuscript, Agent-A and Agent-B. It reproduces the assessor and generator prompts verbatim and lists the settings and parameters that govern the agents' behavior.
The mathematical model behind those parameters, including its notation and derivation, is given in the section "Formal model of interpersonal behavior".
The formal model represents interpersonal states on a centered grid from -3 to +3.
For communication with the LLM components or for display, these internal states can be mapped onto equivalent alternative codings.
In the generator, the seven states are represented by an index-based mapping from 0 for the lowest state to 6 for the highest state, with each index linked to a named behavioral anchor.
The assessor instead returns an integer from 1 to 7.
For reporting in the main text, both are mapped back onto the centered -3 to +3 grid (generator index minus 3; assessor score minus 4).
From the second turn onward, both agents' assessors score each message; the update uses the partner's score, and the assessed scores shown in the main text are averaged across both assessors.
Everything below is extracted from the configuration files that were used to run the agents.
Prompts are quoted unchanged.
Headings, explanations and table captions are editorial.
The prompts are not stored as finished texts.
They are assembled at runtime from named blocks, in the order given by the prompt_creation_order field of the respective component.

This modular structure keeps the source files compact by avoiding repeated prompt text and makes the system flexible, as study-wide, agentspecific, and parameter-specific elements can be changed independently without rewriting complete prompts.

Three levels of configuration contribute: • config.yaml at the study level holds the assessor configuration in full, the study-wide generator blocks, the two personality axes with their rule blocks and state contents, and the language model settings.

• config.yaml inside each agent folder holds the agent-specific generator blocks (description, priority rules, context, biography, situation) and the configuration of the feedback shown to a participant after an interaction.
• One template file per agent folder holds the three free parameters per axis: the behavioral default, the interpersonal reactivity and the repertoire width.
Agent-A is the agent configured in the folder "Bar David Meyer" and is called David Meyer in its own prompts; Agent-B is the folder "Bar John Doe" and is called John Doe.
The two agents share one scenario, a first meeting in a bar, and differ in the three parameters per axis and in the five agent-specific generator blocks (Supplementary Table S1).
